content: Presyncope refers to the sensation of feeling faint, lightheaded, or experiencing muscular weakness without actually losing consciousness. This stage may last only a few seconds and often serves as a prodrome to syncope, which involves a complete loss of consciousness. The most common cause of presyncope is related to cardiovascular issues. Presyncope can be classified into subtypes based on the underlying mechanism that leads to transient global hypoperfusion. It is typically associated with global cerebral hypoperfusion or a toxic/metabolic derangement. Hypoperfusion is most often caused by a drop in blood pressure. The pathophysiology of presyncope involves the interaction between the circulatory system and the autonomic nervous system. The autonomic nervous system plays a critical role in maintaining internal homeostasis, including the regulation of blood pressure, heart rate, fluid and electrolyte balance, and body temperature. Syncope or presyncope occurs due to brain hypoxia, which is usually secondary to a reduction in cerebral perfusion pressure. However, not all reductions in blood pressure result in brain hypoxia, as cerebral circulation is autoregulated to maintain constant brain perfusion despite significant changes in mean blood pressure. This autoregulatory mechanism ensures that regional cerebral blood flow remains stable within a cerebral perfusion pressure range of 50 to 150 mmHg or a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 60 to 160 mmHg. When MAP or cerebral perfusion pressure falls below this range, syncope occurs due to brain hypoxia. Upon standing, gravity causes 500 to 800 mL of blood to pool in the veins below the heart level, increasing capillary pressure and leading to plasma loss into the interstitial fluid. This pooling reduces venous return to the heart, decreasing cardiac output and triggering compensatory mechanisms to maintain arterial pressure. These mechanisms include increased sympathetic outflow mediated by the central autonomic network (CAN), the venoarterial reflex, skeletal muscle leg pumping, cerebral autoregulation, and, to a lesser extent, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). The sympathetic nervous system is the primary effector in the hemodynamic response to postural stressors. Upon standing, reduced cardiac filling and stroke volume are detected by pressure receptors in the heart, carotid arteries, and aortic arch, which send signals to the CAN. This initiates sympathetic vasomotor outflow, releasing norepinephrine to vascular beds in skeletal muscles and cutaneous vasculature, causing vasoconstriction, venoconstriction, and increased heart rate and contractility. Venoconstriction helps correct orthostasis by increasing cardiac filling despite gravitational pooling of blood. Simultaneously, skeletal muscle leg pumping enhances venous return, and the venoarterial reflex augments arterial vasoconstriction in response to venous distension. Postural stress in the atrium is sensed by mechanoreceptors as decreased atrial stretch, leading to increased secretion of arginine vasopressin (AVP) and decreased secretion of A-type atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP). This results in anti-natriuresis, which increases extracellular fluid volume and cardiac filling. The pathophysiology of syncope is summarized as a reduction in systemic blood pressure, leading to decreased global cerebral blood flow and subsequent loss of consciousness. A sudden cessation of cerebral blood flow for 6 to 8 seconds has been shown to cause loss of consciousness. Presyncope can be caused by various factors, including a temporary drop in blood pressure, dehydration, prolonged standing, intense nausea or pain, hypoglycemia (with or without diabetes), neurally mediated hypotension (causing blood pressure to drop upon standing), vagal presyncope, medication side effects, or cardiac arrhythmias. Differentiating presyncope from other conditions that mimic loss of consciousness can often be achieved through a detailed clinical history, though it may sometimes be challenging. Presyncope can occur in patients of all age groups. The prevalence of syncope causes varies depending on the clinical setting and the patient's age. Approximately 19% of the U.S. population will experience a syncopal event in their lifetime, with most occurring in early adulthood or after age 70. Nearly 58% of patients with syncope are female. Syncope accounts for 3% of emergency department visits and up to 6% of hospital admissions in the U.S. Reflex syncope is the most common cause, followed by syncope secondary to cardiovascular disease. Cardiovascular causes are more frequent in older patients and in cardiology-oriented settings. Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is rare in patients under 40 but common in the elderly. Misdiagnosis of non-syncopal conditions as syncope is more frequent in emergency referrals, reflecting the multifactorial complexity of these patients. The high rate of unexplained syncope justifies the need for improved diagnostic strategies. In elderly patients, multiple causes are often present, and their medical history may be less reliable than in younger individuals. There are no established risk factors for presyncope, though occupational, environmental, genetic, and viral factors may play a role. Routine screening for presyncope is not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence. If left untreated, presyncope may progress to syncope, leading to actual loss of consciousness. Common complications include major trauma from falls, sudden cardiac death, seizures, and recurrent hospitalizations. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause. Patients with structural heart disease or primary electrical disease are at high risk of mortality and sudden cardiac death. Morbidity is associated with recurrent episodes and physical injury. Young patients with psychiatric conditions have high rates of recurrent pseudosyncope. Major trauma occurs in 7% of cases, and in older patients with carotid disease, the rate is 43%. Morbidity is particularly high in the elderly, often leading to loss of confidence, fear of falling, depression, fractures, and institutionalization. Diagnosis of presyncope is based on a thorough medical history, including preexisting conditions such as diabetes and heart disease, and a review of medications. Physical examination is essential and should include blood pressure measurements in both arms and in supine and standing positions. Signs to look for include dehydration, flushing, carotid bruits, cardiac murmurs, abdominal masses, varicose veins, and signs of endocrine disorders in the skin, eyes, and thyroid. Carotid sinus massage (CSM) is indicated in patients over 40 with unexplained presyncope after initial evaluation. An electrocardiogram (ECG) may help identify the cause of presyncope, particularly in cases of arrhythmic presyncope. ECG monitoring methods include Holter monitoring, in-hospital monitoring, event recorders, external or implantable loop recorders (ILRs), and remote telemetry. Echocardiography or ultrasound can aid in diagnosing presyncope due to structural heart disease, such as severe aortic stenosis, obstructive cardiac tumors or thrombi, pericardial tamponade, aortic dissection, or coronary artery anomalies. It is recommended when structural heart disease is suspected but is not beneficial unless cardiac etiology is suspected. The tilt test evaluates autonomic neural regulation of cardiovascular orthostatic responses by moving a patient from a supine to an upright position. Assessment of global autonomic function may also help diagnose presyncope etiology through maneuvers like the Valsalva maneuver and pressor testing. Treatment of presyncope involves conservative/nonpharmacologic therapy and medical treatment, depending on the underlying cause. Pharmacologic therapy is recommended for recurrent episodes despite adequate conservative measures and includes beta-blockers, fludrocortisone, midodrine, calcium channel blockers, anticholinergic agents, and serotonin transporter inhibitors. Conservative therapy includes lifestyle modifications, such as avoiding triggers (e.g., heat, prolonged standing, large meals, alcohol), increasing salt and fluid intake, reducing antihypertensive medications, and performing physical counterpressure maneuvers (e.g., leg crossing, squatting). Compression stockings and abdominal binders may help in cases of postural hypotension or venous pooling. Elevating the head of the bed may benefit patients with supine hypertension and postural hypotension. Secondary prevention includes patient education about triggers and management strategies to prevent syncope or orthostatic intolerance.
